tei:titleStmt.tei:title: תחנה אמהות
Teḥinah Imahot for Shabbat Mevorkhim by Leah Horowitz in her Yiddish translation (ca. 1790) with its posthumously expanded adaptation

tei:div.tei:head: Teḥinah Imahot for Shabbat Mevorkhim by Leah Horowitz in her Yiddish translation (ca. 1790) with its posthumously expanded adaptation

tei:lg.tei:l: Master of the universe, ruler of the world! Almighty God, in your great mercy with but ten pronouncements you created, in the first six days, heaven, earth, and all of creation. On the seventh day, that is the Shabbat Qodesh (the holy sabbath) you ceased speaking and you also made it so that your beloved people Yisrael (through whom you are to be glorified, [as it says in the verse] ‘Yisrael, in whom I glory’ (Isaiah 49:3), which translates into Yiddish, ‘You, beloved people of Yisrael, through you am I glorified’) on Shabbat Qodesh should also rest from all work and from superfluous talk. They should only speak words of Torah and study, each according to his ability. Moreover, those [men] incapable of study, and women, should read in Yiddish so they also will understand how to serve God. They must know how to keep the mitsvot that apply to them that God has set forth.

In addition, you have given us new moons which the Sanhedrin would use to sanctify the new months. Today we sanctify the month as we [declare] the month that it will be on the sabbath. That hour is a time when we should pray intensely. Therefore we lay out our pleas before God and pray that you should return us to Yerushalayim and renew our days as of old, for we have no more strength to bear the torments of this hard, bitter exile. Also, we are as sleeping lambs. Our sabbaths, festivals, and months are disrupted. We are like orphans, like sheep lost without a shepherd. For the nations have too much power over us.

But you are ‘the God of Vengeance’. Indeed, God, you always vindicate [us] and make a reckoning with the wicked. Thus we beseech you, Master of the universe, vindicate us against those who harm us. By the merit of the patriarchs and the matriarchs, you, God, as fully as you answered our fathers so should you answer us this month by the merit of our mother — Sarah, for whose sake you declared and said: ‘Do not touch my anointed ones’, which translates: ‘O nations, you dare not touch my righteous ones.’
No nation can have any power to harm her children because of the merits of our mother — Rivqah, who arranged for our father Yaaqov to receive the blessings from father Yitsḥaq.

May these blessings soon be fulfilled for her children Yisrael, by the merit of our faithful mother — Raḥel, you promised that by her merit we the children of Yisrael would come out of exile. Then when Yisrael was sent into exile they were led not far from the grave where our mother Raḥel lies. Israel begged the enemy to allow them to go to Raḥel’s grave. Yisrael came to our mother Raḥel and began to cry and scream, ‘Mother, Mother! How can you watch as we are being led away from you into exile?’

Raḥel went up to Hashem yitbarakh with a bitter cry and declared: ‘Master of the universe! Your mercy is much greater than the mercy of humans. In that respect, I had mercy on my sister, Léah, when my father made the switch and gave her to my husband. He instructed her so that my husband would think that she was I. Although this caused me great sorrow, I told my sister the signals. How much the more so, you, God, are merciful and compassionate. You should simply have mercy and take us out of the exile now.’

It should come to pass by her merit and the merit of our mother Léah: who cried day and night that she not meet the fate of [marrying] the evil Esav; so much that her eyes went dark. By her merit should you enlighten our eyes out of the dark exile.
We indeed shall be known as the daughter of Avraham. The children of Avraham our father, we today should be in his merciful hand.
Wash us thoroughly of our sins for we have been mightily thrashed for our sins. Therefore renew us and bring us in this month to gladness, that all should be turned for the good.
Pride of our strength, you are our great ruler. You will raise us up and turn everything to the good by the merit of the pious, holy patriarchs, Avraham, Yitsḥaq, (and) Yaaqov.

Master of the universe, you have called us ‘my treasure’. That translates, ‘You are my beloved people’. We call you our beloved Father and ask that you grant us and all who apply themselves to your holy Torah—who expound on the holy books and who compose prayers and supplications for us—[that we] should merit having proper and healthy offspring. They should be Torah scholars who serve God with a pure heart, with love, together with the pious. Amen. May it be his will.

tei:note.tei:p: This cataloguing of the merits of the matriarchs as the basis for Yisrael deserving divine favour is a standard trope in tkhines (see NLI R8°894501: Eyn gor sheyne tkhine; cf. the various tkhines in Klirs et al. (eds.), The Merit of Our Mothers). Weissler emphasized that the tkhine genre in general used images that related to women’s identity and implied women’s importance and power (see e.g. Weissler, Voices of the Matriarchs, 7, 48–50, 59–65, et passim).
See Gen. 27:3–18; cf. the blessing associated with Rebecca in the Aramaic text (Aramaic Piyut, Section J) and the analysis below [found in the text of Moshe Rosman’s article].

This paragraph conflates and embellishes several midrashic motifs concerning the matriarch Rachel (see Louis Ginzberg, Legends of the Jews, 6 vols. (Philadelphia, 1954–61), i. 415, ii. 135, iv. 310, and references; see also analysis below).
